story.hook: The Hotel Gave Away Our Paid Room
story.script: We arrived at the hotel just after nine at night after a six-hour drive, tired enough that even the lobby sofa looked comfortable. I handed the front desk clerk our confirmation number, and she stared at the screen for a few seconds before saying there was a problem. Apparently the room we had fully prepaid three weeks earlier was no longer available. I asked what that meant, because I could still see our reservation in the hotel app. She said they had overbooked and another guest had already been given the last room in our category. Then she smiled and told me the good news was that they had one suite left. For a moment I thought she was offering it as the obvious replacement. Instead she turned the monitor toward me and showed an extra charge of nearly three hundred dollars. She said I could pay the difference or they could cancel my reservation and refund me in five to ten business days. I honestly thought I had misheard her. I pointed out that we had already paid, had arrived before the check-in cutoff, and had never been told the room was at risk. She repeated that the only room left was the suite and said upgrades were not complimentary. My partner quietly pulled out the booking email while I asked for a manager. A few minutes later a man came out, listened for maybe twenty seconds, and immediately backed up the clerk. He said overbooking happens in the hotel business and guests sometimes have to accept alternatives. I asked what alternative he was actually offering, because charging me more money for the hotel's mistake did not sound like one. He shrugged and said those were the options. That was when I noticed a small sign on the counter advertising a hotel guarantee that said confirmed prepaid bookings would be honored or the hotel would arrange equivalent accommodation at no additional cost. I pointed directly at it. The manager looked at the sign, then at me, and said that policy depended on availability. I asked him to show me where the sign said that. He could not. Instead he said he was not going to argue in the lobby and offered to cancel us immediately. I told him not to cancel anything and called the chain's customer service line while standing right there. I explained the situation, read them the guarantee word for word, and gave them the manager's name when they asked who had refused to honor it. The call took less than ten minutes. Suddenly the manager's phone rang behind the desk. His whole expression changed while he listened. He put the phone down, disappeared into the office, and came back holding two key cards. The suite was now ours at no extra charge. But it did not end there. Customer service had also refunded our first night because of the delay and added enough loyalty points for another free stay. The manager slid the keys across the counter without saying much. As we walked toward the elevator, the clerk quietly apologized and said they had been told earlier to try charging upgrade fees before offering compensation. The next morning I checked my email and found a written apology from the hotel's regional office. They said the property had handled an overbooking incorrectly and confirmed the guarantee applied exactly as the lobby sign described. So the hotel tried to charge us three hundred dollars for fixing its own mistake, and instead we ended up in the suite, got the first night refunded, and left with enough points for another trip.

youtube.description: Our prepaid hotel room disappeared, and the hotel's fix somehow came with another bill.
